node-1.label: Patient experienced post-procedural abdominal pain, nausea, and elevated body temperature (maximum 37.8°C)

node-2.label: 66-year-old female with history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and thrombocytopenia; routine blood tests over years showed leukocytopenia and thrombocytopenia; initial blood test showed leukocyte count 3.16×10^9/L and platelet count 109.00×10^9/L; no other symptoms and no significant abnormalities in cardiac enzymes or blood coagulation

node-3.label: Four hours post-procedure, patient developed intermittent abdominal pain and occasional nausea; nine hours post-operation, right abdomen pain recurred and progressed to involve the entire abdomen, with persistent nausea and perceived increase in body temperature

node-4.label: Initial physical examination showed tenderness in right abdomen without rebound tenderness or muscular tension and with normal bowel sounds

node-5.label: Later physical examination showed diffuse tenderness with rebound tenderness mainly in right abdomen, dullness to percussion, no liver percussion pain, negative shifting dullness, and normal bowel sounds; maximum body temperature was 37.8°C

why.why: CT showing edematous thickening of the ascending colon with exudative changes and small ascites directly supports peritoneal inflammation, and ascites culture growing Escherichia coli confirms bacterial peritonitis. Baseline leukocytopenia, progressive abdominal pain, and rebound tenderness further support this diagnosis. Expert analyses from both the laboratory physician and radiologist converge on post-procedural peritonitis, with no imaging evidence of perforation or hemorrhage.

CT shows no significant intra-abdominal fluid/blood accumulation, and physical examination showed negative shifting dullness and normal bowel sounds, making significant hemorrhage very unlikely. Expert laboratory and radiology analyses both explicitly state that the absence of significant hemoperitoneum rules out hemorrhage. With a confirmed infectious source, confidence is reduced to 0.03.

CT shows no perforation signs or free air, and the initial examination lacked rebound tenderness and muscular rigidity, making perforation very unlikely. Expert radiological analysis explicitly excludes perforation based on the absence of free air. Confidence is therefore reduced to 0.03.

node-9.label: CT shows edematous thickening of ascending colon with exudative changes and small ascites, without perforation signs or free air

node-11.label: CRP is 2.45 mg/L and PCT is 0.58 ng/ml, showing mild inflammatory elevation

node-12.label: CT shows no significant intra-abdominal fluid or blood accumulation suggestive of hemorrhage

why.why: Ascites culture growing Escherichia coli, CT showing ascending colon edematous thickening with exudative changes, and clinical signs of peritonitis (progressive abdominal pain, rebound tenderness, fever) directly support E. coli peritonitis. Expert laboratory and radiology analyses confirm this diagnosis, and the additional finding of neutrophilia in the setting of baseline leukocytopenia further corroborates infection. Hemorrhage and perforation are excluded by CT, so confidence is increased from 0.9 to 0.95.
